questions.q: Which work area would you use to load and reconcile a bank statement?
questions.explain: Statement loading, reconciliation, and bank/branch/account setup all live in the Cash Management and Banking work area.

questions.q: What problem does routing certain transactions through a cash clearing account solve?
options: It eliminates the need for a GL cash account
It bridges the timing gap between when a transaction is recorded and when the bank actually clears it
It removes the need for bank account security
It automatically converts foreign currency transactions
questions.explain: A clearing account holds amounts like outstanding checks until the bank confirms they cleared, keeping the GL cash balance comparable to the bank's balance.

questions.q: Which object carries the routing or transit number used to route money to a specific location?
questions.explain: The Bank Branch carries routing-level detail such as a routing/transit number, address, and supported payment methods.

questions.q: Which privilege is required to modify the User and Role Security tab on a bank account?
questions.explain: The Manage Bank Account Security privilege specifically controls who can modify a bank account's User and Role Security tab.

questions.q: Which bank statement format is the most common standard for US bank statements?
questions.explain: BAI2 (Bank Administration Institute, version 2) is a plain-text, line-based format that originated in the US and remains the most common US statement format.

questions.q: In BAI2, which numeric range generally represents debit (money-out) summary and detail codes?
questions.explain: 401-699 are debit summary and detail codes, following 400 (total debits summary); 101-399 are the credit equivalent.

questions.q: During which step does Oracle check that the account number on a statement maps to a real Bank Account record?
questions.explain: Import is the validation step, where account mapping, duplicate checks, and conversion into usable records all happen.

questions.q: What does an 'out-of-balance' statement error indicate?
options: The statement was loaded on the wrong day
The bank account's currency was changed
The account has too many transaction codes
The sum of transaction lines doesn't reconcile to the stated opening and closing balances
questions.explain: An out-of-balance statement means the lines don't sum correctly to the file's own stated balances — a sign of a corrupted file or parsing problem.

questions.q: What is the correct resolution when a bank statement line has no system counterpart because the transaction was never entered into Oracle?
options: Record the missing transaction in the appropriate subledger
Escalate it to the bank as an error
Apply an account-level tolerance rule to ignore it
questions.explain: A missing transaction should be recorded (or confirmed as pending entry), not forced into a match against something that doesn't exist.

questions.q: In the worked example, what explained Harborview Metals Inc.'s $4,200 difference?
options: Already-reconciled transactions that hadn't yet run through that day's Create Accounting process
questions.explain: Both other reports showed everything accounted for on the system and statement side, pointing to a pending Create Accounting run as the explanation.

questions.q: A tolerance rule associated with a matching rule can only apply when the matching rule's match type is which of these?
questions.explain: Tolerance is only applied when the matching rule is a One to One match type; other match types don't support an associated tolerance.

questions.q: Why does even a high-volume account, mostly handled by automatic reconciliation, still rely on manual reconciliation?
options: It doesn't — high-volume accounts never need manual reconciliation
To handle the exceptions automatic reconciliation couldn't confidently match
Because automatic reconciliation is always disabled on high-volume accounts
Because manual reconciliation runs before automatic reconciliation
questions.explain: Manual reconciliation is where exceptions left behind by automatic reconciliation get resolved, regardless of the account's overall volume.

questions.q: For which kind of cash flow is trend-based (historical) forecasting especially useful?
options: Only categories with zero historical data
Only transactions already reconciled to a bank statement
Cash flow categories, like retail cash sales, that don't show up as a clean open transaction but follow a predictable pattern
questions.explain: Trend-based forecasting projects past actuals forward, which is useful for cash flows without a corresponding open system transaction.

questions.q: Why can the Cash to General Ledger Reconciliation report (Lesson 14) show a temporary difference even when nothing is actually wrong?
options: Because the report is always inaccurate
Because Cash Positioning overwrites the GL balance
Because bank statements are never loaded correctly
Because a transaction can be reconciled but not yet have gone through Create Accounting
questions.explain: A reconciled transaction awaiting its Create Accounting run produces exactly this kind of temporary, explainable gap.

questions.q: Why is a cash position only as reliable as the reconciliation work behind it?
options: Because reconciliation and positioning are entirely unrelated processes
Because the position leans on real, reconciled statement balances — stale unreconciled items distort the picture
Because a cash position ignores bank statements entirely
Because positions are only built once a year
questions.explain: Since the position is built on real reconciled activity, an account with a backlog of stale unreconciled items will show a distorted, unreliable position.

questions.q: What must happen to an external transaction before it can be accounted?
options: It must be reconciled against the bank statement
It must be converted to a different currency
It must be approved by Receivables
questions.explain: Like other Cash Management transactions, an external transaction must be reconciled before the Create Accounting process can post it.
